run.question: List the top 5 largest Elasticsearch indices matching the pattern 'app-184-*' by document count. Show their names and doc counts.

report.summary: Querying the Elasticsearch target m0-otel-20260909 for indices matching 'app-184-*' and sorting by docs.count descending, the five largest indices are app-184-ml-worker-2024.01.25, app-184-data-analytics-2024.01.10, app-184-engineering-api-2024.01.20, app-184-security-auth-2024.01.05 and app-184-platform-billing-2024.01.15, each with docs.count 500 (all health green, status open). The next rows in that same descending order drop to docs.count 1, so the five 500-document indices sit alone at the top of the sampled ordering; their relative order among themselves is a sort tie with no meaning. The read slice of the sorted result covers only rows 0-9 of 1800 total_rows (truncated true), so the claim that nothing else exceeds one document rests on the sort order rather than a per-row check of all 1800 indices. One tooling caveat: without sort=docs.count:desc the docs.count column projected as null and a jq filter on it matched nothing, so doc counts were only readable in the tool's sorted output. These are index-level statistics observed at query time (2026-11-23T17:25-17:26Z), not document counts within any incident window, and no service health conclusion follows from them.

claims.text: In the descending-docs.count listing for pattern 'app-184-*', the rows returned were app-184-ml-worker-2024.01.25 (docs.count 500, store.size 47.9kb), app-184-data-analytics-2024.01.10 (500, 46.9kb), app-184-engineering-api-2024.01.20 (500, 31.1kb), app-184-security-auth-2024.01.05 (500, 46.9kb) and app-184-platform-billing-2024.01.15 (500, 46.8kb), all health=green status=open, followed immediately by app-184-ml-billing-2024.01.09, app-184-data-db-2024.01.34, app-184-ml-billing-2024.01.08, app-184-data-db-2024.01.35 and app-184-ml-billing-2024.01.07 at docs.count 1.
The sliced read of that listing covers returned rows 0-9 of slice.total_rows 1800 and is marked truncated true with 1790 rows omitted, so only the top ten rows of the ordering were inspected.

A separate sorted listing (columns index,docs.count) independently returned app-184-ml-worker-2024.01.25, app-184-data-analytics-2024.01.10 and app-184-engineering-api-2024.01.20 as rows 1-3, each with docs.count "500", consistent with the read slice.

Tool behavior observed: when the listing was requested without sort=docs.count:desc, the docs.count field came back null in jq (type 'null'), and a jq filter selecting rows with docs.count == "500" returned count 0 and an empty names list, i.e. doc counts were only readable via the tool's sorted output.

The five top indices share an identical docs.count of 500 while their store sizes differ (47.9kb, 46.9kb, 31.1kb, 46.9kb, 46.8kb), which is consistent with uniform fixture-seeded indices rather than differing activity; this is inference from the counts and sizes alone.

gaps: The read slice of the sorted listing is truncated (returned 10 of 1800 rows; 1790 omitted), so rows beyond the top ten were not inspected individually and the 'nothing else above 1 document' reading rests on sort order, not per-row verification.
Ordering among the five 500-document indices is a sort tie and carries no meaning; a re-query could return a different order within the tie.
docs.count could not be read without sort=docs.count:desc (null in jq), so no independent jq-side max or count of large indices was obtainable.

The first listing attempt for this pattern exceeded the response size limit and returned status error (RESULT_TOO_LARGE, 1800 rows, 68799 tokens), so that unsliced result could not be cited directly and only its sliced read was used.
These are index statistics at query time (2026-11-23T17:25-17:26Z); the tool has no time range, so counts during earlier parts of the authorized window are unknown.
